The corpus contains HippoRAG (not a distinct 'HippoRAG 2') and WiCER (the wiki compile-evaluate-refine system, which appears to be what 'WikiLoop' refers to). They differ sharply in whether downstream feedback is used at all.

HippoRAG: no downstream feedback loop. It builds its structured knowledge base (an LLM-extracted OpenIE knowledge graph plus synonymy edges) once, offline, and uses it only at retrieval time via Personalized PageRank over query-linked nodes [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4]. All components are used off-the-shelf without fine-tuning, and errors (48% NER, 28% OpenIE, 24% PPR) are diagnosed but not fed back to repair the graph [2405.14831#s21.p2][2405.14831#s32.p5]. The graph is a static index, not an artifact refined by query outcomes.

WiCER/WikiLoop: feedback is the core mechanism. It treats the compiled wiki as a lossy abstraction and runs a compile-evaluate-refine loop: probe the wiki (one diagnostic probe per source document, or the real query stream in deployment), and any probe scoring 1/5 triggers diagnosis of the specific dropped facts, which are fed back as explicit preservation constraints in the next compilation [2605.07068#s36.p1][2605.07068#s5.p1]. This instantiates CEGAR, with a score-1 probe as counterexample and pinning as refinement; pinned facts cannot be lost again, so the failure set shrinks monotonically [2605.07068#s37.p1][2605.07068#s61.p4]. Diagnosed pinning gains +0.95 over blind compilation vs +0.16 for random pinning (5.9×), recovering 80% of lost quality and cutting the score-1 rate from 55.1% to 24.8% [2605.07068#s41.p4][2605.07068#s39.p2].

In short: HippoRAG uses a fixed, one-shot extracted graph purely for retrieval, with no downstream-feedback repair; WikiLoop/WiCER uses downstream probe failures as counterexamples to iteratively repair and pin facts in its compiled knowledge artifact.

When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and makes explicit, conflict-targeted write-side decisions about older memories: it decides whether they remain usable, should be revised, or should be blocked before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Memory entries are marked active or stale, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked unknown-current [2605.06527#s15.p1]. The key design principle is that new evidence should not only produce a new memory entry but also trigger explicit decisions about older states that may no longer remain usable [2605.06527#s62.p1]. Invalidation need not occur in the same slot as the new evidence, so CUPMem builds a bounded candidate set from directly affected and propagation-affected regions, with the adjudicator making the final retirement decision [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At query time, only authorized memories ground generation: active items serve as current grounding, stale items are treated as historical context, and unresolved slots prevent an unsafe old default from being used as a premise [2605.06527#s15.p1].

CUPMem handles older memories at write time via state adjudication rather than at query time. An LLM adjudicator evaluates each candidate old state and assigns it KEEP, STALE, REPLACE, or UNKNOWN, giving new evidence write-side authority [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Stale states are archived rather than deleted, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked UNKNOWN_CURRENT [2605.06527#s63.p10]. A topology-triggered search expands the candidate set beyond directly touched slots to structurally affected state regions, so propagated conflicts (e.g., a relocation invalidating commute assumptions) are retired before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At readout, active items ground answers, stale items serve as historical context, and unresolved slots block unsafe old defaults; queries presupposing an invalidated state are blocked and the current basis is reconstructed from active memories [2605.06527#s15.p1]. All modifications obey temporal causality: only later evidence may revise or archive earlier items [2605.06527#s64.p19]. This raises overall accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% under the same GPT-4o-mini backbone [2605.06527#s15.p1].

They operate at different levels. HippoRAG (2) is a non-parametric continual-learning retrieval framework: new information is handled by expanding the offline index — an LLM extracts OpenIE triples and passages become passage nodes linked by context edges, with synonym edges added by embedding similarity [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. It has no explicit conflict-resolution or invalidation mechanism; retrieval is query-to-triple matching plus LLM triple filtering and Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. GC-Mem, by contrast, is an inference-time consistency protocol for mutable RAG: it targets Semantic Shadowing, where updated entity states leave old contradictory chunks in the store and dense retrieval returns the stale majority [2609.16073#s2.p2]. It runs a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies a temporal dominance operator that excises any chunk contradicted by a newer one, so the terminal state wins [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. GC-Mem's effectiveness is bounded by detector recall (>50% required) [2609.16073#s20.p1][2609.16073#s16.p3], whereas HippoRAG's design concern is retrieval quality across factual, associative, and sense-making memory rather than contradiction handling [2502.14802#s2.p6][2502.14802#s14.p8].

When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and makes explicit, conflict-targeted write-side decisions about older memories—deciding whether they remain usable, should be revised, or should be blocked before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Memory entries are marked active or stale, and unsafe slots without a settled replacement are marked unknown-current [2605.06527#s15.p1]. The key design principle is that new evidence should not only produce a new memory entry but also trigger explicit decisions about older states that may no longer remain usable [2605.06527#s62.p1]. Invalidation need not occur in the same slot as the new evidence, so CUPMem builds a bounded candidate set from directly affected and propagated (affected) regions plus global candidates, with the adjudicator making the final retirement decision [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At query time, only authorized memories ground generation: active items serve as current grounding, stale items are treated as historical context, and unresolved slots prevent an unsafe old default from being used as a premise [2605.06527#s15.p1].

CUPMem handles older memories at write time rather than at query time: an LLM adjudicator assigns each candidate old state one of KEEP, STALE, REPLACE, or UNKNOWN [2605.06527#s15.p1]. Stale states are archived rather than deleted, and slots without a settled replacement are marked UNKNOWN_CURRENT [2605.06527#s63.p10]. A topology-triggered search then expands invalidation to structurally affected state regions, so propagated conflicts are retired before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At readout, only authorized state is consumed: active items ground answers, stale items serve as historical context, and unresolved slots block unsafe old defaults [2605.06527#s15.p1]. This raises overall accuracy from 8.7% to 68.0% under the same GPT-4o-mini backbone [2605.06527#s15.p1].

The later paper extends the loop by predicting likely counterexamples from the news stream and preemptively refining, rather than waiting for a failed QA probe: "rather than waiting for a counterexample (failed QA probe), we *predict* likely counterexamples from the news stream and preemptively refine" [2606.09877#s11.p1]. The key conceptual shift is that a counterexample is no longer an observed failure (a score-1 probe revealing a fact lost in the compiled wiki) but a *predicted* future failure derived from the incoming news stream [2606.09877#s11.p1]. In WiCER, the counterexample is a diagnostic probe that scores 1, confirmed spurious because the fact exists in the document collection but was lost in the compiled wiki [2605.07068#s37.p1].

WiCER's loop is reactive: it evaluates the compiled wiki with one diagnostic probe per source document, and a score-1 probe acts as the CEGAR counterexample, triggering diagnosis of dropped facts and pinning them as preservation constraints [2605.07068#s36.p1][2605.07068#s37.p1]. Streaming Knowledge Compilation (Online WiCER) replaces this probe-driven reactive pinning with proactive pinning driven by a predicted materiality signal φ̂_t, which scores a document's importance for an entity and serves as a query-relevance surrogate, so facts are pinned before any query exposes a gap [2606.09877#s2.p3][2606.09877#s2.p5]. It also adds decay-weighted eviction and periodic full recompilation every T_r steps, with O(√(T log K)) regret plus a prediction-error term [2606.09877#s31.p2][2606.09877#s43.p3]. The key conceptual shift is 'predictive CEGAR': the counterexample is no longer an observed QA failure but a predicted high-materiality news item, moving refinement from diagnosis to prediction [2606.09877#s42.p1][2606.09877#s42.p4].

Agent Zero Memory treats knowledge updates as versioned, provenance-bearing assertions rather than silent overwrites: it records each assertion with origin, immutable timestamp, and evidence pointer, and its citation-locked reading discipline structurally excludes fabrication [2608.29606#s6.p2][2608.29606#s6.p3][2608.29606#s6.p4]. It explicitly criticizes systems that "overwrite silently or accrete contradictions" and identifies epistemic loss when updates overwrite rather than version as a failure axis [2608.29606#s1.p2][2608.29606#s3.p7]. Its design principle is that memory should maintain a durable, queryable, honest model of what is known — layering raw sources, curated facts, and inferred experience, with provenance and calibrated belief under the citation lock, and no single organizing structure serving all question types [2608.29606#s1.p3][2608.29606#s6.p5].

Raw-RAG takes the opposite stance: it indexes raw, unprocessed history with no LLM extraction, summarization, graph construction, or mutation, and leaves resolution of temporal order and state changes (including superseded facts) to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. It argues mutation is largely unnecessary — UPDATE/DELETE are only 4.39% of LoCoMo and 2.46% of LongMemEval write decisions, and replacing UPDATE with ADD and DELETE with NONE actually raises LoCoMo accuracy from 67.36% to 69.42% [2610.30755#s2.p3][2610.30755#s2.p6]. Its design principle is simplicity/evidence preservation: retrieval over raw history with strong evidence coverage (45.29% MemoryAgentBench, 76.35% MEME) and path coverage (62.34%) beats complex agentic memory in six of seven settings, and adding atomic-fact extraction, summarization, or graph expansion hurts accuracy [2610.30755#s1.p1][2610.30755#s12.p1][2610.30755#s15.p7][2610.30755#s16.p3].

In short: Agent Zero versions and provenance-locks updates (supersession-friendly, honest belief modeling), while Raw-RAG avoids mutation entirely and relies on raw evidence plus reader-side state reconstruction.

In short: HippoRAG associates passages via read-time graph propagation (PPR over an LLM-extracted KG) to enable multi-hop retrieval, whereas TOKI resolves contradictions via write-time bitemporal operators with declared isolation levels and audit logging, not via graph traversal.

The two papers treat the link differently: the Missing Knowledge Layer paper makes persistence semantics the organizing principle and treats contradiction resolution as a consequence of the Knowledge layer's supersession semantics, while TOKI treats contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control whose correctness depends on declared isolation and audit persistence.

Missing Knowledge Layer: it argues CoALA and JEPA conflate knowledge with memory, producing a category error where systems apply cognitive decay to factual claims or treat facts and experiences with identical update mechanics [2604.11364#s1.p1]. Its fix is four layers with distinct persistence semantics: Knowledge is indefinite and updated by supersession (append-only + provenance), Memory decays (Ebbinghaus) with bi-temporal event sourcing, Wisdom is durable and revision-gated, Intelligence is ephemeral [2604.11364#s7.p3]. Crucially, knowledge facts are superseded, not forgotten: old claims are preserved and linked to successors with provenance [2604.11364#s8.p1]. So contradiction resolution is subsumed under persistence: supersession is the Knowledge layer's persistence mechanism, and the four-layer count is claimed as the minimum decomposition where each layer needs a different persistence mechanism [2604.11364#s16.p1]. It notes BEAM at 10M tokens shows all systems scoring worst on contradiction resolution (<0.05) and temporal reasoning (0.12), abilities requiring architectural rather than retrieval solutions [2604.11364#s13.p6], and its pilot improved contradiction resolution 0.500 vs 0.394 with oracle typed routing [2604.11364#s20.p9].

TOKI: it argues contradiction resolution in LLM-agent persistent memory is write-time concurrency control, and that the four shipped heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) are one family of bitemporal operators, each with an undeclared isolation precondition and undeclared admitted write-time anomalies [2606.06240#s1.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. Persistence here means the bitemporal fact (valid-time, system-time, provenance, confidence) [2606.06240#s6.p1] plus a dual-row schema with a current/audit discriminator, where default retrieval filters to current rows and audit rows reach through a separate slice [2606.06240#s9.p1]. Each operator returns a winner with a system-time invalidation of the loser and emits an audit tuple [2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s10.p2]. It identifies LLM-specific anomalies including audit erasure N3 (loss of the overwritten fact) [2606.06240#s11.p1], and audit erasure is universal among baselines with a documented provenance path (five of six) [2606.06240#s17.p4]. The audit-row defence moves its primary LoCoMo slice by Δ=+0.86 [2606.06240#s18.p3].

In short: the Missing Knowledge Layer paper derives contradiction handling from layer-specific persistence semantics (supersession vs decay), whereas TOKI specifies contradiction resolution as a write-time operator contract whose soundness is tied to isolation level and to durable audit persistence of overwritten facts.

RAPTOR builds a tree by clustering chunks of text, summarizing each cluster, and repeating this bottom-up to create a tree that captures both high-level and low-level details, enabling questions to be answered at different levels [2401.18059#s2.p4]. Its summarization step sends each cluster's nodes to a language model to produce concise summaries [2401.18059#s10.p1], and the cycle of embedding, clustering, and summarization continues until further clustering is infeasible, yielding a multi-layered tree [2401.18059#s8.p3].

RAPTOR (Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval) [2401.18059#s1.p1]. It recursively embeds, clusters, and summarizes chunks of text, building a tree bottom-up where each parent node summarizes a cluster of children [2401.18059#s2.p2][2401.18059#s8.p3], and at inference retrieves across abstraction levels so questions can be answered at different levels of detail [2401.18059#s1.p1][2401.18059#s11.p7].
